articles.title: How We Cut the Coupling Tax in a Post-Booking API
articles.basis: Title only — the article body could not be read (Medium and Agoda's careers blog both block automated access). The concepts below are my explanation of the term, not the article's content: read the article and compare.
articles.says: Agoda published how a post-booking API (the APIs used after a booking exists: status, details, changes, cancellations — what partners and internal services call) was decoupled from the systems behind it. The article's specific design is not summarised here because it could not be read.
concepts: Coupling tax

The cost every consumer pays when it depends on a provider's internals: each change in the booking model forces changes, testing and coordinated releases in everyone who calls it. The "tax" grows with the number of consumers.
Consumer-shaped read model
Instead of every caller querying the booking core, publish booking changes as events and build a view shaped for post-booking reads. The core can change its tables without breaking callers.
Anti-corruption layer / stable contract
A boundary that translates the internal model into a versioned external contract, so internal refactors stay internal.
Backend-for-frontend
One thin API per kind of consumer (app, partner, support tool), each owning its own shape, instead of one API that must satisfy everybody.
articles.say: "Partners and post-booking tools shouldn't pay a coupling tax on the booking core — I'd give them a versioned contract over an event-fed read model, so the core's schema can change without a coordinated release. Agoda has written about cutting exactly this tax in a post-booking API."

articles.title: How Agoda's Multi-Product Booking Engine Powers Seamless Travel Bookings
articles.basis: Search summaries of the article + press coverage of the May 2026 launch (WiT, PR Newswire).
articles.says: The booking engine (MPBE) behind "One Checkout" — hotels, flights and activities in one transaction — is a graph of small asynchronous agents. Each agent is a single-responsibility module that reacts to signals from the engine; each product has a predefined graph, and a multi-product booking merges them into one graph managed by orchestrator components. Shared steps such as payment happen once, not per product; the system chooses a safe confirmation order instead of confirming everything in parallel; bookings are processed in-region; OpenTelemetry, Pyroscope and dashboards give observability.
concepts: Workflow as a graph of agents
The booking is a graph of steps (reserve flight, reserve hotel, charge, confirm). Agents own one step each and react to events, so a new product adds nodes, not a new monolith.
Safe confirmation order
With several suppliers, confirm the riskiest or least cancellable item first, so a later failure is cheap to undo — a saga ordering decision.
Do shared steps once
Payment and fraud checks run once per checkout, not once per product.
articles.say: "For a multi-product booking I'd model the flow as a saga graph and pick a safe confirmation order — confirm what is hardest to cancel first. Agoda's One Checkout engine merges per-product graphs and runs payment once for the whole basket."

articles.title: Booking Deduplication: How Agoda Manages Duplicate Bookings Across Multiple Data Centers (Parts 1–2)
articles.basis: Search summaries of both parts + daily.dev summary.
articles.says: Duplicate bookings came from incidents and slow confirmations (customers rebooking). The old deduplication only worked inside one data center because it used data created there. The new design keeps local databases per DC plus a central database with data from all DCs; the deduplication service reads both. Hashing booking data unified deduplication across products (one table, one service instead of one per product). The same approach — SQL unique key constraints and isolation levels — was later reused for API-request and message deduplication.
concepts: Idempotency across data centers
A retry or a rebook can land in another DC; a uniqueness check that only sees local data misses it. You need a shared (central) view or a key that routes to one owner.
Content hash as a dedup key
Hash the fields that make two bookings "the same" (guest, property, dates, amount) so one generic service can deduplicate any product.
Unique constraint as the lock
Let the database reject the second insert with the same key — the cheapest correct duplicate check.
articles.say: "A client-supplied idempotency key handles retries, but customers also rebook when confirmation is slow — that needs content-based dedup, and across data centers it needs a central view. Agoda's dedup service checks both local and central stores with a hashed booking key."

articles.title: How We Built a Scalable and Reliable Platform to Support Millions of Travelers
articles.basis: Search summary of the article (an interview with a Director of Engineering).
articles.says: Agoda runs mainly on its own on-premise infrastructure. At checkout, priorities shift from traffic volume to consistency of data stored in different regions — every transaction matters. When payment gateways or suppliers have temporary problems, workflows queue and retry the transaction automatically, so bookings become consistent for the customer even through interruptions.
concepts: Different consistency per stage
Search optimises for volume and latency; checkout optimises for correctness. Saying where the line is shows Staff judgement.
Queue-and-retry for external failures
A booking that hits a gateway outage is parked durably and retried with backoff, not failed — eventual consistency the customer can live with.
articles.say: "Search is about throughput, checkout is about correctness — so checkout gets durable queues and retries around gateways and suppliers. Agoda describes exactly that split."

articles.title: A Deep Dive into Agoda's Generic Reconciliation Platform
articles.basis: Search summaries of the article + Agoda careers page summary.
articles.says: Several team-built reconciliation frameworks (no standards, not scalable) were replaced by one generic platform. Data from two sources lands in big-data tables; a separate Normalizer transforms both into a standardised table; the platform matches records by a key (e.g. partner_id must match before records are compared), supports manual force-reconciliation, writes reports to big-data tables, and is monitored by three services. Spark is the engine; hundreds of reconciliation jobs run in production, runtimes stay under a couple of hours, and a new reconciliation can be onboarded within a month (Spark, Vast, Hadoop, Oozie, Kubeflow).
concepts: Normalise first, then match
Two sources never agree on format; a normaliser into one canonical table makes the matcher generic.
Comparability key
Decide which fields must match before two records are even compared (partner, booking id); everything else is a difference to classify.
Platform, not one-off scripts
Reconciliations become configuration on a shared engine, which is how one team supports hundreds of jobs.
articles.say: "I'd normalise both sides into a canonical table, match on a comparability key, classify every difference, and run it as a generic Spark job — that's how Agoda's reconciliation platform runs hundreds of reconciliations."

articles.title: How Agoda Enhanced the Uptime and Consistency of Financial Metrics (FINUDP)
articles.basis: InfoQ (Jan 2026) and ByteByteGo summaries + search summary of the article.
articles.says: Multiple independent pipelines produced inconsistent financial numbers. Agoda consolidated them into a centralised Spark platform (the Financial Unified Data Pipeline) as one source of truth, with a multi-layer quality framework: automated validations, ML-based anomaly detection and data contracts, over millions of daily booking transactions. The stated trade-off: any change needs testing and a data-quality check of the whole pipeline, which slows velocity.
concepts: Single source of truth
One pipeline owns a metric; downstream consumers read it instead of recomputing it.
Data contracts
Producers promise a schema and semantics; a breaking change fails a check instead of silently corrupting reports.
Named trade-off
Centralising trades team velocity for consistency — saying the cost is the Staff part.
articles.say: "For money metrics I'd have one pipeline own the numbers with data contracts and anomaly checks, and accept slower change as the price — Agoda made exactly that trade with its unified financial pipeline."

articles.title: PriceAggregator: An Intelligent System for Hotel Price Fetching (Parts 1–3: SmartTTL, SmartScheduler)
articles.basis: Search summaries of the series + the arXiv paper (2008.02087).
articles.says: Agoda cannot call suppliers on every search, so prices come from a cache; a miss means no price shown, and over 20% of searches can fail to get a supplier price. A fixed TTL trades hit rate against staleness. SmartTTL assigns a TTL per itinerary from clustered price-change behaviour (check-in date is among the strongest features). SmartScheduler proactively refreshes entries nearing expiry within supplier budgets. Reported A/B results: SmartTTL +2–4% cache hit rate and about +2% bookings; SmartScheduler over +10% bookings vs an LRU-based baseline.
concepts: TTL is a business trade-off
Too short: more misses and supplier calls; too long: stale prices and failed bookings. Different itineraries deserve different TTLs.
Adaptive TTL
Learn how fast prices change per segment (near-term dates change faster) and set TTLs from that.
Proactive refresh within a budget
Spend limited supplier calls on the entries most likely to be requested and about to expire.
articles.say: "A single TTL is wrong for supplier prices — near check-in dates change faster. I'd set TTLs per segment and spend the supplier budget refreshing hot entries before they expire; Agoda published this as SmartTTL and SmartScheduler, with measurable booking gains."

articles.title: How Agoda Scaled Its Price Cache with DragonflyDB
articles.basis: Search summaries of the article + InfoQ and daily.dev coverage.
articles.says: The Price Cache holds terabytes of volatile supplier rate data (InfoQ: about 1.5 TB) and moved from 72 SQL Server shards to DragonflyDB, whose shared-nothing multi-threaded design shards the data internally. Reported: roughly 8× better P99 read latency, about 300K requests/s at around 8 ms P99. The migration ran dual reads — SQL Server kept serving while the Price API also read DragonflyDB asynchronously — until parity passed 99.9%, then traffic moved gradually through an A/B experiment over several weeks. Two clusters provide high availability.
concepts: Shadow / dual reads
Read from the new store in parallel without serving from it; compare results until parity is proven.
Gradual cut-over by experiment
Move a percentage of traffic at a time and watch business metrics, with instant rollback.
A cache that is the dataset
When a cache holds the full working set, sizing and memory-safety thresholds become capacity planning, not tuning.
articles.say: "To change the store behind a hot cache I'd run dual reads until parity is above 99.9%, then shift traffic gradually as an experiment — the way Agoda moved its 1.5 TB price cache off 72 SQL Server shards."

articles.title: Improving Performance Using Distributed Cache with Couchbase
articles.basis: Search summaries of the article.
articles.says: Hotel metadata moved from a local in-process cache to a distributed Couchbase cache, plus pre-caching. Cold starts had caused misses and database surges. A scheduled producer, pre-cache builders (consumers) and a Kafka queue keep the cache filled; total response time dropped by roughly 20%. The accepted trade-off: metadata can be stale until a builder refreshes it.
concepts: Local vs distributed cache
Local caches are fast but small, duplicated per instance and cold after every deploy; a distributed cache is shared and survives restarts.
Pre-caching (cache warming)
Fill the cache ahead of demand from a queue so users never pay for the miss.
Staleness is the price
Say how stale is acceptable and how refresh works.
articles.say: "Per-instance caches go cold on every deploy and hammer the database; I'd use a shared cache warmed by a producer/consumer job, accepting bounded staleness — Agoda reported about 20% faster responses doing that for hotel metadata."

articles.title: Feature store at Agoda: ScyllaDB as the source of truth, DragonflyDB as the cache (and a Rust serving layer)
articles.basis: Search summaries of the Dragonfly and Rust articles + HackerNoon / The New Stack coverage.
articles.says: The online feature store serves millions of requests per second with a P99 target around 10 ms. DragonflyDB is a non-persistent central cache; on a miss the service reads ScyllaDB, the source of truth. A classic cache stampede hit: bursts of identical requests all reached ScyllaDB at once, and retries kept the pressure up. One network-tuning change cut P99 from over 40 ms to 2.2 ms. Coverage credits NVMe upgrades, cache work and data modelling with a 50× scale-up; serving was rewritten in Rust for latency.
concepts: Cache stampede
Many requests miss the same key at once and all hit the database. Fix with single-flight (one loader per key), jittered TTLs and early refresh.
Retries amplify overload
Retrying into an overloaded store makes it worse — combine with backoff, budgets and coalescing.
Cache is never the source of truth
Here explicitly: the cache is non-persistent; ScyllaDB is the truth.
articles.say: "Hot keys expiring together cause a stampede, and retries make it worse — I'd coalesce loads per key and jitter TTLs. Agoda hit this exact stampede in its feature store in front of ScyllaDB."
more: Why Agoda bet on Rust for the feature store

articles.title: How Agoda manages 1.8 trillion events per day on Kafka
articles.basis: Search summaries of the article + ByteByteGo coverage.
articles.says: About 1.8 trillion events a day (later coverage: 3 trillion records). A two-step logging design: a client library writes events to local disk and a separate Forwarder daemon ships them to Kafka, so producers are isolated from Kafka outages. Clusters are split by use case rather than one big cluster per DC. Load balancing is lag-aware (consumers and producers react to lag instead of static partition assignment). Kafka feeds about half of the data going into the warehouse.
concepts: Write locally, forward asynchronously
The request path writes to local disk; a daemon forwards — a Kafka hiccup never blocks a user request.
Clusters per use case
Blast-radius control: a noisy analytics topic cannot hurt booking events.
Lag-aware balancing
Route work away from consumers that are falling behind instead of assigning partitions evenly and hoping.
articles.say: "I wouldn't make the request path depend on the broker — write locally and forward, like Agoda's client-plus-Forwarder design at over a trillion events a day — and split clusters by use case to contain blast radius."

articles.title: How Agoda Handles Kafka Consumer Failover Across Data Centers
articles.basis: Search summaries of the article + InfoQ coverage.
articles.says: Kafka runs in several on-prem data centers. A stretch cluster was rejected because latency between distant DCs is too high. Data is mirrored (MirrorMaker 2), and a custom service synchronises consumer-group committed offsets and OffsetSync records both ways, so a consumer group can fail over to the other DC and fail back, with only one active consumer group per DC pair at a time. Translating offsets between clusters was the hard part.
concepts: Replicating data is not enough
For failover you also need consumer positions; offsets differ between mirrored clusters, so they must be translated.
One active consumer per pair
Avoid two DCs processing the same stream at once — a fencing rule for active-passive.
Failback is a design step
Plan how offsets flow back when the primary returns.
articles.say: "Active-passive messaging needs offsets, not just data — mirror topics, translate offsets both ways, and make sure only one DC's consumers are active. Agoda built exactly that on MirrorMaker 2 because a stretch cluster was too slow across their DCs."

articles.title: How Agoda Solved Retry Storms to Boost System Reliability
articles.basis: Search summaries of the article.
articles.says: Agoda added Envoy's retry budget to a custom fork of Istio. During a downstream slowdown, retries reached about 8% of request volume against a 5% budget and the budget rejected the excess, protecting the downstream service; a counter tracks retries skipped because the budget or a circuit breaker was exhausted. A budget computed per service let heavy endpoints use far more than intended, and deriving budgets from Envoy's cluster-level statistics was hard.
concepts: Retry storm
Every layer retrying turns a slowdown into an outage: 3 layers × 3 retries = 27× load.
Retry budget
Retries may be at most a percentage of active requests (e.g. 5%); beyond that, fail fast.
Measure the overflow
Count retries that were not attempted, so you can see the budget working.
articles.say: "Per-call retry counts multiply across layers; I'd cap retries with a budget — a percentage of live traffic — at the mesh, and alert on budget overflow. Agoda added Envoy retry budgets to Istio after seeing retries hit 8% of traffic."

articles.title: How Agoda Handles Load Shedding in Private Cloud (Gatekeeper)
articles.basis: Search summaries of the article.
articles.says: Load shedding used to rely on per-pod configuration limits that were often set too high — it worked only when configured correctly, and several incidents followed. Because shedding ran as middleware inside JVM services, a garbage-collection pause also paused the shedding. Agoda moved towards service-agnostic load shedding (outside the application) to prioritise critical traffic during unexpected load.
concepts: Load shedding
When overloaded, reject low-priority requests early (cheaply) so high-priority ones still succeed — better than everyone timing out.
Shed outside the process
In-process shedding freezes with the process (GC pauses); a proxy or sidecar keeps working.
Static limits drift
Hand-set thresholds go wrong as hardware and code change; prefer adaptive limits (concurrency/latency based).
articles.say: "Under a spike I'd shed low-priority traffic at the edge or sidecar with adaptive limits, not hand-tuned per-pod numbers — Agoda found in-process shedding stops during GC pauses."

articles.title: How We Eliminated Configuration-Related Outages and Scaled Consul Management at Agoda
articles.basis: Search summary of the article + daily.dev summary (figures from the latter).
articles.says: Consul configuration replicated instantly to all four data centers, with no validation and no audit trail — risky at scale. Agoda moved to GitOps: changes go through Git and code review, a sync service validates them against auto-generated JSON Schemas before applying them to Consul. Reported scale: 34,000+ key-value pairs, 100+ changes a day, 100+ teams onboarded, a full audit trail; per-data-center rollout was the next step.
concepts: Config is code
Review, validate and audit configuration changes like code — a bad config is the most common cause of global outages.
Instant global replication is a risk
Roll configuration out per data center (canary) instead of everywhere at once.
articles.say: "Config changes are the classic global outage, so I'd ship them through review with schema validation and roll them out one data center at a time — Agoda moved its 34K Consul keys to GitOps for exactly this."

articles.title: How Agoda Simulates Booking Flows to Test Flight Integrations
articles.basis: Search summaries of the article + ZenML case summary.
articles.says: A connector layer sits between Agoda and each flight supplier: request/response mapping, error handling, multi-call coordination and retries. End-to-end testing is mandatory for every new connector (search → booking → cancellation), but full production-like stacks made it slow. A simulator with a Workflow Executor plays the surrounding system and drives the connector through its internal contract instead.
concepts: Connector / adapter per supplier
Each supplier's protocol, quirks and errors live in one module behind one internal contract.
Contract-level simulation
Test a connector by simulating its neighbours, not by standing up the whole platform.
articles.say: "Each supplier gets an adapter behind one internal contract, and I'd test adapters against a simulator of that contract — Agoda simulates whole booking flows to certify new flight connectors."

articles.title: Inside Agoda's Content Enrichment Platform: Managing 450M+ Property Images
articles.basis: Search summaries of the article + press coverage (Aug 2025).
articles.says: 450M+ property images are enriched by offline Spark applications that add ML-derived metadata (tags from visual content); the platform was rebuilt as a monorepo, adding a model is mostly configuration, and replication went from months to minutes. Press coverage adds detecting low-resolution images and enhancing them, removing duplicates, and ranking images by clarity and relevance.
concepts: Offline enrichment, online serving
Heavy ML runs in batch over the catalogue; serving reads precomputed tags.
Configuration over code for new models
A platform where a new model is a config change scales to many teams.
articles.say: "I'd run ML enrichment offline over the catalogue and serve precomputed tags — Agoda enriches 450 million property images that way."

articles.title: Inside Agoda's Private Cloud (The Pragmatic Engineer, 2 parts) + How Agoda Transitioned to Private Cloud
articles.basis: Pragmatic Engineer summaries + Agoda's own private-cloud articles (search summaries).
articles.says: Agoda runs its own private cloud: four data centers (US, Europe, two in Asia), co-located; the largest about 1 MW; ~7.5M QPS database load at peak; 20–30 PB of data; Kubernetes-based compute platform ("Fleet"); worker nodes of 44, 64 or 96 cores, with hardware generations differing by up to 30% in throughput per core — so replica counts are a poor capacity measure.
concepts: Capacity in cores, not replicas
When hardware differs, plan capacity in normalised compute, not pod counts.
Multi-DC by default
Every design at Agoda's scale must say what happens when one of four data centers is gone.
articles.say: "At Agoda's scale — four data centers and millions of queries a second — I'd state the failure domain up front: what this service does when one DC disappears."
more: How Agoda transitioned to private cloud

articles.title: Supporting more than 200 payment methods globally
articles.basis: Title, author and date from search results only; the article body could not be read (Medium blocks automated reading).
articles.says: Agoda's payments engineering wrote about supporting more than 200 payment methods across its markets. The body was not readable here, so this card gives the design problem the title describes, not the article's own solution: many local methods (wallets, bank transfers, pay-later) through several providers, each with different flows and failure modes.
concepts: One payment API, many adapters
Checkout sees one contract; each provider or method sits behind an adapter that normalises requests, errors and webhooks.
Methods as configuration
Which methods appear in which country, currency and amount range is data, so launching a method is not a checkout release.
Asynchronous methods
Redirect, QR and bank-transfer methods complete later: a pending state with an expiry, completed by webhook or poll.
articles.say: "Agoda has written about supporting 200+ payment methods; at that count the only sane shape is one payment API, a method catalogue as config, and one adapter per provider behind a router."

articles.title: Agoda's virtual card programme for paying hotel partners (J.P. Morgan case study)
articles.basis: Search summary of the J.P. Morgan case study and coverage; not an Agoda engineering article.
articles.says: Agoda settles with hotel partners by virtual card and bank transfer. In 2020 it moved to a self-issued virtual card model licensed by a card network, with J.P. Morgan as settlement bank; coverage reports self-issuance in 50+ currencies. A 2026 Checkout.com announcement says virtual card issuing will also process payouts to hotels and other travel partners.
concepts: Card as a control
A card per booking, capped to the amount and valid from check-in, lets the card network enforce the payable.
Pay in the supplier's currency
Issuing in the hotel's currency moves FX handling to Agoda, where it is measured in the ledger.
Reconcile against network files
What the hotel actually charged arrives in card network settlement files, matched to payables.
articles.say: "Agoda pays many hotels by virtual card — publicly described as self-issued in 50+ currencies — so I'd issue one card per booking capped to the payable and reconcile against the network's settlement files."

articles.title: Agoda's payment partners: orchestration (Juspay) and acquiring/issuing (Checkout.com), and its payments strategy (Primer interview)
articles.basis: Partner case studies and a Primer interview with Agoda's payments lead, via search summaries. These are vendor-published, so they describe the partner's view.
articles.says: Partner case studies describe Agoda handling a complex, fragmented payment landscape in Asia with an orchestration partner, and a 2026 Checkout.com partnership focused on payment performance (approval rates) for acquiring and issuing. Primer's interview with Agoda's payments lead discusses building the payment strategy at scale. Treat the numbers in vendor case studies as marketing until checked.
concepts: Approval rate is revenue
A point of authorisation rate on large volume is worth more than most infrastructure savings; routing and retries are business features.
Orchestration vs build
Partners give methods and routing quickly; owning the payment model and the routing data keeps control.
Vendor evidence is one-sided
Cite it as 'publicly described', never as measured fact.
articles.say: "Agoda publicly works with orchestration and acquiring partners, which tells me approval rate is treated as revenue — so the router ranks routes by live approval and cost, and we keep the payment model ourselves."
more: Primer: Dipa Dubhashi on Agoda's payment strategy

themes.name: Correctness at checkout, volume at search
themes.why: Search tolerates stale, cached prices; booking and payment do not — dedup across DCs, queue-and-retry, single source of truth for money.

themes.name: Supplier calls are the scarce resource
themes.why: Cache supplier prices, set TTLs by how fast prices change, refresh within a budget, and isolate each supplier behind a connector.

themes.name: Caches are never the source of truth
themes.why: Distributed caches with warming; stampede control; dual reads to migrate; a durable store behind every cache.

themes.name: Multi-data-center by default
themes.why: Four DCs: dedup needs a central view, Kafka failover needs offset translation, config rolls out per DC.

themes.name: Overload protection is designed, not hoped for
themes.why: Retry budgets at the mesh, service-agnostic load shedding, a Forwarder so producers never block on Kafka.

themes.name: Money moves in many currencies through many partners
themes.why: One payment API over 200+ methods, partners for acquiring and orchestration, hotels paid by self-issued virtual cards, and one reconciliation platform proving it all.

themes.name: Decouple consumers from the core
themes.why: Post-booking consumers on contracts and read models; workflows as agent graphs; platforms (reconciliation, enrichment) instead of one-off code.
